PUBLIC WORKS-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 3, 1985, I put a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) concerning the proposal submitted by this Government to the expropriated Mirabel landowners, because all my constituents of Argenteuil-Papineau are directly concerned with this issue.
Mr. Speaker, on the day following the signature of a Memorandum of Agreement between the CIAC and this Government on the rectifying of that gigantic blunder, it seems most important to me that this House should be cognizant of this comprehensive proposal, in view of the astronomical costs to the public treasury of maintaining and managing those lands, namely some $50 million a year. Located some 45 minutes away from Montreal, in between the four major centres of Saint-Jerome, Saint-Eustache, Sainte-Therese and Lachute, the prime farmlands of Mirabel, comprising over 2,500 UTH, had shaped its people to the image of a prosperity.
Progress, however, had decided that in this area favoured by nature, agriculture should give way to something else. The
Adjournment Debate
mere mention of that progress now puts the whole people on edge. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, in 1969, with one stroke of a pen this Government decision put an end to those 150 years of tradition and brought the whole Mirabel area back to the year 1867 by degrading its residents and landowners down to the level of tenants. Canada's biggest expropriation operation, second only to the one that dispossessed the Indians, brought havoc in the lives of approximately 10,000 people living in twelve villages or fourteen municipalities, covering an area as wide as the lie Jesus. It does not happen every day that 97,000 acres of land suddenly change hands.
And the new owner was not easy to get along with. In sixteen years, he changed faces and policies a number of times. There were seven successive directors, delegated by the Federal Government to manage the land and the people in the Mirabel reserve.
One such director stated he had no authority to make decisions. Another acted in a more high-handed way. What one allowed, the next one forbade. Leave given by one director was not valid in the eyes of another. At times there were written permissions, at other times oral permissions, or benevolent silence with indications to proceed as before.
Mr. Speaker, it is in such a climate of confusion and insecurity that my constituents in Mirabel have had to survive, waiting for the situation to clear up and become normal again. It is not easy to live in expectancy during sixteen long years.
Mr. Speaker, the Mirabel tragedy is that the area has ceased to live and progress for fifteen years. During all those years, a prosperous and promising area was literally sacrificed to the ambition of an incompetent and hard-nosed Government. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the displacement of 10,000 persons and especially the social disruption of 97,000 acres present a situation almost identical to that of the displaced persons in Europe following the Second World War, or to the deportation of the Acadians.
The impact of such a social upheaval cannot be assessed, especially in such an economically and demographically integrated area.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec farming communities, economic and social life is, to a great extent, related to agricultural activities. The land is set aside for agricultural use and the village is the focus of services and business; it is also the preferred setting for retirement or for those who do not earn their living directly through farming.
Like everywhere else, the villages acquired the services and businesses they needed. The village of Sainte-Scholastique, because of its geographical location, had become a major agricultural centre for other villages. The presence of two doctors, two notaries, one pharmacist, four grocery stores, three hardware stores and a farm equipment dealer shows how important this centre was in 1969. The structure of these parishes based on networks of near neighbours, relatives,

March 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
friends, services and mutual assistance was destroyed by the upheaval which followed this mass expropriation. People became strangers in their own neighbourhood.
Fences were no longer repaired and buildings were left to rot because people understood that any action might mean rent increase.
What about the municipal representatives who had to live with federal interference in municipal affairs during all those years? This municipality has fallen into a state of collapse and it will have to be untiring in its efforts to give back Mirabel the prosperity which was expected following the construction of the airport.
In 1976, half of the people had left, and in 1979, a survey showed that, among the 2,130 families residing in the area at the time of the expropriation, only 250 families of farmers or their sons and about 250 families of residents or businessmen were still there. Torn between their deep social roots and their need for stability, the residents and businessmen or their children, who feel less bound by their investment than the farmers, now account for only 20 per cent of the residential population of the area, while 90 per cent of those expropriated or their children who were still farming in the area in 1979 are still there.
Another survey published in 1983 depicts the situation as follows: number of farms expropriated in 1969, 858; number of residences occupied in 1969, 788, and in 1983, 555; number of residences destroyed, 233; number of barns occupied in 1969, 731, and in 1983, 455; number of barns destroyed, 276; number of farmers in 1969, 788, and in 1983, 251; number of businesses in 1969, 146, and in 1983, 98; number of residences in 1969, 1045, and in 1983, 816.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, the whole population of the Argenteuil-Papineau constituency, and especially my constituents in Mirabel felt a great deal of emotion yesterday at the announcement of the agreement arrived at by my Government, which succeeded in solving this issue after only six months through consultation and dialogue. Can the Minister tell the House the terms of this historical agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Roch La Salle (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-EXPROPRIATION OF LAND AT MIRABEL- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to answer the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) and I also wish to congratulate her on the interest she has shown in this case since she was elected on September 4. Mr. Speaker, before elaborating on the main recommendations of the agreement proposed yesterday by the two parties and jointly signed by them, that is, by the Canada Lands Company (Mirabel) Limited and the CIAC-the expropriated farmers-I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to join the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau in saying that for a long time, I found it very sad that the Government had failed to act responsibly with respect to the surplus property around the Mirabel project-christened Mirabel sixteen years ago. In this lovely setting, even lovelier in the past, I was very moved to see how much these people had suffered as a result of expropriation, and especially their disappointment in the previous Government's failure to take any action, especially since we managed to reach a settlement in less than five months. I remember I had a very special interest in this question, being well acquainted with the farming milieu and with rural ridings. Yesterday, I had the privilege of attending the gathering that took place at Mirabel and giving these people the assurance of my support for a proposal that was negotiated in less than five months. I also wish to pay tribute to my Director General, Mr. Hardy, who replaced the board of directors of the company shortly after September 4, and who did a tremendous job, and also to those people who led the struggle to get back their land, and I would like to mention, of course, Mrs. Rita Lafond, Mr. Jean-Paul Raymond and Mr. Andre Bouvette who were very important to this cause, and all those who were members of the board of directors or the administration of CIAC.
It is therefore clear, Mr. Speaker, that we have safeguarded this great principle I have always defended: first refusal goes to the expropriated farmer, and otherwise, the land will be sold back to the tenants. Still, a number of measures will be taken to help expropriated owners get and buy their land back; tenants will be looked after as well since anyone who, for valid reasons, does not want to buy back the property will not be asked to vacate the premises before two years, and in no instance will the rent go up before two years.
The importance and relevance of agricultural development has been the subject of discussion, of course, and it was pointed out that those lands were, if I may put it that way, good examples of prime agricultural soil. We made sure of that in the general agreement which I will submit to my Cabinet colleagues for official signature within a few weeks. All those people have been told that we will cooperate with the Quebec Government to promote agricultural recovery.
I would be remiss if I failed to mention the excellent cooperation I got from the Minister of Agriculture of Quebec throughout this major consultation, because those are indeed prime agricultural lands. Mr. Speaker, we may have reached this equitable, reasonable and humanitarian settlement, in any case I think we did our best to be fair, but it remains quite clear that we will never be able to compensate for the harm done to those people, and I am very sorry about that. I do not find any satisfaction in the fact that I cannot be held responsible. Unfortunately, I was witness to everything those people had to put up with, but I am pleased that at last we have found a solution which I think will be accepted by my Cabinet colleagues within a few weeks. Again it will be with great pleasure that I will go back to Mirabel shortly with the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau to present them with an official signature on behalf of the Canadian Government.
March 28, 1985

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEVERANCE PAY MEASURES. (B) PURPOSE AND TREATMENT OF SEVERANCE PAY
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEVERANCE PAY MEASURES. (B) PURPOSE AND TREATMENT OF SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments this evening relate to a question I asked of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) on March 8. At that time I asked whether she was prepared to postpone the implementation of the severance pay provision of the Unemployment Insurance Act whereby it was provided that severance pay must first be used up before unemployment insurance benefits could be paid.
That was announced on November 8 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Originally it was supposed to come into effect on December 31, 1984. That announcement was made without one iota of consultation. The decision to use severance pay in calculating unemployment insurance benefits was a decision made unilaterally by the Government, I think specifically by the Minister of Finance. I think the Minister of Employment and Immigration had very little to do with it and that the Minister of Finance announced it without any consultation.
That is one of the problems with the particular program. We on this side of the House believe that there should have been consultation, and the Government says it believes in consultation and consensus. Yet, no consultation was undertaken by the Government, by the Minister of Finance or by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. She did not consult with the organized trade union movement because, if she had, it would have raised all sorts of problems with the implementation of such a provision.
As a result of the announcement on November 8, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and back-bench Tories were inundated with protests from various groups and individuals across the country. As a result, the Minister acceded to extending the implementation of the provision until April 1, 1985.
There was a second problem with that particular announcement. No impact studies were made. The announcement was made without any study of the group or the people who would be impacted by such a decision. In fact, no studies were conducted to discover the effects of such a provision on unemployed people. If they had done such studies, they would have found out that severance pay was a lump sum amount of money paid to an employee when an employer gives him the golden handshake and says "Goodbye, your services are no longer required". Many Canadians who find themselves in that unfortunate predicament often take their lump sum payment and roll it into an RRSP to help them in their retirement years. This Government believes in self-reliance. In this particular circumstance when folks are being retired by their employers and are being told that they are no longer needed they are not in fact being allowed to look after their retirement years.
Adjournment Debate
Also they could have found out that persons who are laid off and receive severance pay immediately attempt to find work. They use their severance pay as a form of mobility; they use the money to move around. Maybe they have to leave their communities to look for work. In fact Employment and Immigration Centre mobility programs do not provide grants for unemployed people, so the severance pay becomes a very important form of income for them while they go out and look for work. Now the Government is saying that severance pay must be used for day to day living before they can collect unemployment insurance. It is cruel, it is unjust and it is unfair.
Once again we call upon the Government to postpone, or, in fact, to cancel the whole idea until it has conducted the proper consultation and studies. Then it can bring something to the House, and we will see whether we can support it at that time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEVERANCE PAY MEASURES. (B) PURPOSE AND TREATMENT OF SEVERANCE PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a question of equity.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act regulations were announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November last. Those amendments will ensure that all payments drawn from a job are dealt with in the same way under the unemployment insurance system. It seems normal to us. The government considers such a policy as normal. According to the comments of my colleague from Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I should have been swamped with requests. It may be that my constituents have lost my address, but as far as 1 know I have not received a single request from people affected by such a measure. I may have received more in his constituency but for my part, I did not receive any. I wanted to make that correction.
Under the present regulations, Mr. Speaker, the salary drawn by an individual for a part-time jobs is taken in consideration in the computation of unemployment benefits. This is considered a normal practice. It is possible for that individual to look at the same time for a full-time job. Such an amount must be deducted. The benefits are reduced accordingly. However, an individual who draws severance pay or an annuity can receive a second income when applying for unemployment insurance benefits. The proposed amendments are then aimed at putting an end to such unfair treatment. It is quite obvious. The individual can even find a job a few weeks or months later and draw some additional income which would be unfair compared with other Canadians generally.
For the sake of equity and to allow the individuals concerned to adjust to the amendments, some provisions have been passed so that any decision made under the former regulations will be upheld. The regulation concerning the allowance for paid holiday and the severance pay will come into force in a few days, on March 31. All claims submitted

March 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
prior to that date will be treated under the previous regulations, up to the end of the validity period of such claims. In the case of claims submitted after March 31st, 1985, vacation pay and severance pay will be treated as any other form of earned income at the time of determining the entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits. This measure is considered as being fair by the Government.

There is maybe an exception. A transitional provision means that any severance payment made under a collective agreement or special work force reduction agreement in force prior
to December 31, 1984, will also be treated under the regulation.

Mr. Speaker, we feel that this measure is fair and reasonable, and the Government has no intention of changing its views.
